specStatements.text: The elements in the periodic table are arranged in order of atomic (proton) number and so that elements with similar properties are in columns, known as groups. The table is called a periodic table because similar properties occur at regular intervals.
Elements in the same group in the periodic table have the same number of electrons in their outer shell (outer electrons) and this gives them similar chemical properties.
Students should be able to:
explain how the position of an element in the periodic table is related to the arrangement of electrons in its atoms and hence to its atomic number
predict possible reactions and probable reactivity of elements from their positions in the periodic table.
Before the discovery of protons, neutrons and electrons, scientists attempted to classify the elements by arranging them in order of their atomic weights.
The early periodic tables were incomplete and some elements were placed in inappropriate groups if the strict order of atomic weights was followed.
Mendeleev overcame some of the problems by leaving gaps for elements that he thought had not been discovered and in some places changed the order based on atomic weights.
Elements with properties predicted by Mendeleev were discovered and filled the gaps. Knowledge of isotopes made it possible to explain why the order based on atomic weights was not always correct.
Students should be able to describe these steps in the development of the periodic table.
Elements that react to form positive ions are metals.
Elements that do not form positive ions are non-metals.
The majority of elements are metals. Metals are found to the left and towards the bottom of the periodic table. Non-metals are found towards the right and top of the periodic table.
Students should be able to:

explain the differences between metals and non-metals on the basis of their characteristic physical and chemical properties. This links to Group 0 , Group 1 , Group 7 and Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
explain how the atomic structure of metals and non-metals relates to their position in the periodic table
explain how the reactions of elements are related to the arrangement of electrons in their atoms and hence to their atomic number.

The elements in Group 0 of the periodic table are called the noble gases. They are unreactive and do not easily form molecules because their atoms have stable arrangements of electrons. The noble gases have eight electrons in their outer shell, except for helium, which has only two electrons.
The boiling points of the noble gases increase with increasing relative atomic mass (going down the group).
Students should be able to:
explain how properties of the elements in Group 0 depend on the outer shell of electrons of the atoms
predict properties from given trends down the group.
The elements in Group 1 of the periodic table are known as the alkali metals and have characteristic properties because of the single electron in their outer shell.
Students should be able to describe the reactions of the first three alkali metals with oxygen, chlorine and water.
In Group 1, the reactivity of the elements increases going down the group.
Students should be able to:
explain how properties of the elements in Group 1 depend on the outer shell of electrons of the atoms
predict properties from given trends down the group.

The elements in Group 7 of the periodic table are known as the halogens and have similar reactions because they all have seven electrons in their outer shell. The halogens are non-metals and consist of molecules made of pairs of atoms.
Students should be able to describe the nature of the compounds formed when chlorine, bromine and iodine react with metals and non-metals.
In Group 7, the further down the group an element is the higher its relative molecular mass, melting point and boiling point.
In Group 7, the reactivity of the elements decreases going down the group.
A more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive halogen from an aqueous solution of its salt.
Students should be able to:
explain how properties of the elements in Group 7 depend on the outer shell of electrons of the atoms
predict properties from given trends down the group.

scopeNotes.statement: the reactions of the first three alkali metals with oxygen, chlorine and water
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every required Group 1 reaction taught here uses lithium, sodium or potassium only, and only with oxygen, chlorine and water. Rubidium and caesium appear solely as predictions made from the stated trend in reactivity (as 4.1.2.5 'predict properties from given trends down the group' requires), never as reactions students are expected to recall.

scopeNotes.statement: the nature of the compounds formed when chlorine, bromine and iodine react with metals and non-metals
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Compound formation is taught for chlorine, bromine and iodine only. Fluorine and astatine are used only where a trend down the group is being extended by prediction. 'Nature of the compounds' is treated as the specification frames it - ionic with metals, covalent with non-metals - without going into bonding detail that belongs to 4.2.

scopeNotes.statement: predict properties from given trends down the group.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Prediction items always supply the trend or the data on which the prediction rests (for example three measured boiling points, or the stated reactivity trend). Students are never asked to recall values for elements the specification does not require, and correct answers are justified by the trend rather than by remembered data.

scopeNotes.statement: A more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive halogen from an aqueous solution of its salt.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Displacement is presented only for halogens in aqueous solutions of halide salts. No displacement of halogens from solids or melts is taught, and no electrode or redox treatment is introduced, since half equations and oxidation/reduction in these reactions are not part of 4.1.2.6.

concepts.definition: The arrangement of all the elements in order of atomic (proton) number, set out so that elements with similar properties fall in the same column. It is called periodic because similar properties occur at regular intervals.
A column of the periodic table. Elements in the same group have the same number of electrons in their outer shell, and this is why they have similar chemical properties.
A row of the periodic table. The period number tells you how many occupied electron shells the atoms of that element have, so it fixes the element's position from top to bottom.
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom of an element. The modern periodic table places elements in increasing order of atomic number, not atomic weight.
The electrons in the highest occupied shell of an atom. These are the electrons involved in reactions, so elements with the same number of outer electrons behave chemically alike.
The repeating pattern of properties across the table: as atomic number rises, similar properties reappear at regular intervals because the outer electron arrangement repeats.

Using an element's group and its place within that group to work out what it is likely to react with and how vigorously. Elements in the same group react in the same sort of way; the trend down the group sets how vigorous the reaction is.
The method used before protons, neutrons and electrons were discovered: scientists listed the elements in order of their atomic weights and looked for repeating properties.
Spaces Mendeleev deliberately left in his table for elements he thought had not yet been discovered. Elements with the properties he predicted were later found and filled those gaps.
Where strict atomic-weight order put an element in a group whose properties it did not share, Mendeleev swapped the order so that the element sat with elements it resembled.

concepts.term: Isotopes and the atomic weight problem
concepts.definition: An element's atomic weight is an average across its isotopes, so it does not always rise in step with proton number. Once isotopes were known, this explained why the order based on atomic weights was not always correct.
An element that reacts to form positive ions. Its atoms have few outer electrons, which are lost in reactions.
An element that does not form positive ions. Its atoms have outer shells close to full, so in reactions they gain or share electrons rather than losing them.
The majority of elements are metals. Metals lie to the left and towards the bottom of the periodic table; non-metals lie towards the right and top.

concepts.term: Physical properties of metals and non-metals
concepts.definition: Metals are typically shiny, malleable, good conductors of electricity and of thermal energy, and generally have high melting and boiling points. Non-metals are typically dull, brittle when solid, poor conductors, and generally have lower melting and boiling points.

concepts.term: Chemical properties of metals and non-metals
concepts.definition: Chemically the dividing line is ion formation: metals react to form positive ions, non-metals do not. Compounds of a metal with a non-metal are ionic; compounds of two non-metals are covalent.

The number of outer electrons places an element in its group and the number of occupied shells places it in its period. Because the total number of electrons equals the number of protons, position in the table follows directly from atomic number.
The elements of Group 0. They are unreactive and do not easily form molecules because their atoms already have stable arrangements of electrons.
The full outer shell held by noble gas atoms: eight outer electrons, except helium, which has only two. Having no need to lose, gain or share electrons is why Group 0 is unreactive.
The boiling points of the noble gases increase with increasing relative atomic mass, that is, going down the group.
The elements of Group 1. Their characteristic properties come from the single electron in their outer shell, which is lost in reactions to form ions with a 1+ charge.

concepts.term: Reactions of lithium, sodium and potassium
concepts.definition: With oxygen they form white metal oxides (for example 4Li + O2 -> 2Li2O). With chlorine they form white metal chlorides (for example 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl). With water they fizz, giving hydrogen and an alkaline solution of the metal hydroxide (for example 2K + 2H2O -> 2KOH + H2).
Reactivity increases going down Group 1. The outer electron is in a shell further from the nucleus and is shielded by more inner shells, so the attraction on it is weaker and it is lost more easily.

The elements of Group 7. They are non-metals with seven electrons in their outer shell, which is why they have similar reactions, and they exist as molecules made of pairs of atoms, such as Cl2, Br2 and I2.
Chlorine, bromine and iodine react with metals to form ionic compounds - metal halides - in which the halide ion carries a 1- charge, for example sodium chloride, sodium bromide and sodium iodide.
Chlorine, bromine and iodine react with non-metals to form molecular compounds in which the atoms are joined by covalent bonds, for example hydrogen chloride, hydrogen bromide and hydrogen iodide.
The further down Group 7 an element is, the higher its relative molecular mass, melting point and boiling point.
Reactivity decreases going down Group 7. The outer shell is further from the nucleus and is shielded by more inner shells, so an electron is attracted into it less strongly and is gained less easily.

A more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive halogen from an aqueous solution of its salt, for example Cl2 + 2KBr -> 2KCl + Br2. Chlorine displaces bromine and iodine; bromine displaces iodine; iodine displaces neither.

Using a stated pattern down a group, together with data for elements you are given, to work out a property of an element you have not met. The prediction must follow the direction of the trend and be justified by it.

misconceptions.question: Does the group number tell you how many electron shells an atom has?
misconceptions.correct: The group number gives the number of outer electrons; the period number gives the number of occupied shells.
misconceptions.misconception: The group number tells you how many shells of electrons the atom has, and elements next to each other in the same row are the ones that behave alike.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both group and period are labelled with numbers and both describe position, so students who have not linked them to the electronic structure attach the wrong one to shells. Reading the table left to right, like text, also makes rows feel like the natural families.
misconceptions.correction: Count from the electronic structure: 2,8,7 has three occupied shells, so Period 3, and seven outer electrons, so Group 7. Similar properties run down the columns, because it is the outer electrons that control how an element reacts.

misconceptions.question: In the electronic structure 2,8,7, which number gives the outer electrons?
misconceptions.correct: The last number, 7. The number of numbers, 3, gives the period.
misconceptions.misconception: The outer shell is the biggest number in the structure, or the group is given by the period number.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students see 2,8,7 as a list of facts rather than as shells filled in order, so they pick whichever figure looks most important - usually the full shell of 8 - or reach for the period number they have just worked out.
misconceptions.correction: Read the structure as shells filled from the inside out. The final number is always the outer shell and fixes the group; the count of numbers is the number of occupied shells and fixes the period. So 2,8,7 is Group 7, Period 3.

misconceptions.question: Are the elements in the modern periodic table placed in order of relative atomic mass?
misconceptions.correct: They are placed in order of atomic (proton) number.
misconceptions.misconception: The elements are listed in order of increasing mass, so a heavier element always comes later in the table.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Relative atomic mass is printed on the table alongside the atomic number and usually does rise from left to right, so the pattern looks like a mass ordering. It is also the ordering scientists genuinely used before protons were discovered.
misconceptions.correction: The modern order is by atomic (proton) number. Mass usually rises with it but not always, because relative atomic mass is an average over an element's isotopes.

misconceptions.question: Does 'periodic' mean the properties repeat exactly every row?
misconceptions.correct: Similar properties occur at regular intervals, but the intervals are not one row long and the periods are not all the same length.
misconceptions.misconception: Every period contains the same number of elements and the pattern starts again in exactly the same way one row later.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Periodic' is met in maths and physics as a fixed, exact repeat, and the top of the table, where Periods 2 and 3 both hold eight elements, seems to confirm it.
misconceptions.correction: The repeat is of similar properties, not of an identical row. Period 1 holds two elements, Periods 2 and 3 hold eight, and Period 4 holds eighteen once the transition metals appear.

misconceptions.question: Do all the noble gases have eight electrons in their outer shell?
misconceptions.correct: They have eight outer electrons, except for helium, which has only two.
misconceptions.misconception: Every Group 0 atom has a full outer shell of eight electrons, helium included.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The 'stable octet' is repeated so often that students treat eight as a rule with no exceptions, and helium's position at the top right of the table looks like any other Group 0 place.
misconceptions.correction: Helium is 2 - its only shell holds a maximum of two electrons, and two is full for that shell. The specification states the exception explicitly, so it is expected in an answer.

misconceptions.question: Are noble gases unreactive because their outer shells are empty?
misconceptions.correct: They are unreactive because their atoms have stable arrangements of electrons - a full outer shell.
misconceptions.misconception: Noble gases have nothing in their outer shell, so there is nothing there to react with.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students hear 'they do not lose or gain electrons' and conclude there are none to lose. 'Inert' and 'empty' get bundled together as one idea of nothing happening.
misconceptions.correction: The outer shell is full, not empty: eight electrons, or two in helium. A full shell is already stable, so there is no gain in losing, gaining or sharing electrons.

misconceptions.question: Does reactivity increase going down every group of the periodic table?
misconceptions.correct: Reactivity increases down Group 1 but decreases down Group 7.
misconceptions.misconception: Elements get more reactive further down the table, whichever group you are in.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Group 1 is usually taught first and its trend is memorable, so it becomes the default rule. The underlying reason - distance and shielding weaken the pull on outer electrons - is remembered as 'more reactive' rather than as a cause.
misconceptions.correction: The same cause gives opposite trends. Group 1 atoms must lose an electron, and a weaker pull makes that easier, so reactivity rises. Group 7 atoms must gain an electron, and a weaker pull makes that harder, so reactivity falls.

misconceptions.question: Are alkali metals more reactive further down the group because their atoms have more electrons to lose?
misconceptions.correct: Every Group 1 atom loses exactly one electron; reactivity rises because that electron is held less strongly.
misconceptions.misconception: Potassium is more reactive than lithium because a potassium atom has more electrons available to give away.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know atoms get larger with more electrons down a group and reach for the most visible difference. 'More electrons' feels like 'more reaction'.
misconceptions.correction: All Group 1 atoms have one outer electron and lose that one electron only. Further down, the outer electron sits in a shell further from the nucleus with more inner shells shielding it, so it is lost more easily.

misconceptions.question: Which gas is given off when an alkali metal reacts with water?
misconceptions.correct: Hydrogen.
misconceptions.misconception: The bubbles are oxygen, because the oxygen has come out of the water.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Water is known as H2O and students associate bubbling in water with oxygen from lessons on photosynthesis or electrolysis. The metal hydroxide product also contains oxygen, which seems to confirm it.
misconceptions.correction: The metal takes the hydroxide part and releases hydrogen: 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2. The oxygen stays in the hydroxide ion, and the hydrogen given off can be tested with a lighted splint.

misconceptions.question: Do the halogens exist as single atoms?
misconceptions.correct: They consist of molecules made of pairs of atoms, such as Cl2, Br2 and I2.
misconceptions.misconception: Chlorine is just Cl, so an equation can be written as Na + Cl -> NaCl.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The element's symbol on the periodic table is a single letter or two, and the chloride in a compound is written as one atom, so the free element gets written the same way.
misconceptions.correction: Free halogens are diatomic. Any equation must use Cl2, Br2 or I2 and then be balanced: 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl.

misconceptions.question: What type of compound forms when a halogen reacts with a metal?
misconceptions.correct: An ionic compound - a metal halide containing halide ions with a 1- charge.
misconceptions.misconception: Halogens are non-metals and non-metals make covalent compounds, so a halogen makes covalent compounds with everything.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn 'halogens are non-metals' and 'non-metals bond covalently' as separate facts and combine them without checking what the halogen has reacted with.
misconceptions.correction: The bonding depends on the partner. Metal plus halogen gives an ionic compound, because the metal forms a positive ion and the halogen a negative one. Non-metal plus halogen gives a covalent, molecular compound.

misconceptions.question: Is iodine more reactive than chlorine because its atoms are bigger and heavier?
misconceptions.correct: Chlorine is more reactive than iodine; reactivity decreases down Group 7.
misconceptions.misconception: Bigger, heavier atoms must be more powerful, so iodine reacts more strongly than chlorine.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday reasoning equates bigger and heavier with stronger, and the Group 1 trend has already taught students that reactivity rises down a group.
misconceptions.correction: A Group 7 atom reacts by gaining an electron into its outer shell. In iodine that shell is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so an electron is attracted in less strongly. Reactivity therefore falls down the group.

misconceptions.question: Can any halogen displace any other halogen from a solution of its salt?
misconceptions.correct: Only a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one.
misconceptions.misconception: If you mix a halogen with a solution of a different halide, a displacement always happens - they simply swap over.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember 'displacement' as a swap between two similar things rather than as a competition decided by reactivity, so direction feels irrelevant.
misconceptions.correction: The direction matters. Chlorine displaces bromide and iodide; bromine displaces iodide only; iodine displaces neither. Adding bromine to potassium chloride solution gives no reaction, because bromine is less reactive than chlorine.

misconceptions.question: Is an element a metal if it conducts electricity?
misconceptions.correct: An element is a metal if it reacts to form positive ions.
misconceptions.misconception: Conducting electricity is what makes something a metal, so any element that conducts must be a metal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Conductivity is the property students meet first, it is easy to test, and almost all metals do conduct - so the test gets mistaken for the definition.
misconceptions.correction: The specification defines metals by chemistry: elements that react to form positive ions are metals, and elements that do not form positive ions are non-metals. Conductivity is a typical physical property, not the definition - graphite, a form of the non-metal carbon, conducts electricity.

misconceptions.question: Are most of the elements non-metals?
misconceptions.correct: The majority of elements are metals.
misconceptions.misconception: Non-metals outnumber metals, because non-metals are the ones we meet most in chemistry.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Oxygen, carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen and the halogens dominate early chemistry lessons, and the non-metal block at the top right is where most named examples come from.
misconceptions.correction: Count the table: metals occupy the left-hand side, the whole transition block and the bottom, and they are the clear majority. Non-metals are confined to the top right.

misconceptions.question: Why did Mendeleev leave gaps in his periodic table?
misconceptions.correct: He left gaps for elements he thought had not yet been discovered.
misconceptions.misconception: He left gaps to make the table look tidy and symmetrical, or because he could not decide where certain known elements should go.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The finished table looks neat, so the gaps read as a design choice. Students also know he changed the order in places and merge the two actions into one idea of tidying up.
misconceptions.correction: The gaps were a scientific prediction. Mendeleev kept elements with similar properties together and left a space wherever the pattern demanded an element nobody had found. Elements with the properties he predicted were later discovered and filled the gaps.

misconceptions.question: Did Mendeleev arrange the elements in order of atomic number?
misconceptions.correct: He used atomic weights - protons had not yet been discovered.
misconceptions.misconception: Mendeleev built the modern table, so he must have known each element's atomic number.
misconceptions.whyItArises: His table looks very like the modern one, and students see atomic number as such a basic fact that they assume it was always available.
misconceptions.correction: Before protons, neutrons and electrons were discovered, scientists could only classify elements by atomic weight. Ordering by atomic number came later, once subatomic particles were known.

misconceptions.question: Did early scientists classify the elements by grouping them by their properties alone?
misconceptions.correct: They arranged the elements in order of their atomic weights and then looked for repeating properties.
misconceptions.misconception: Before subatomic particles were known, elements were simply sorted into families by how they behaved, with no measured quantity involved.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know the point of the table is to group similar elements, so they assume the grouping came first; sorting by observed behaviour also feels like the natural starting point.
misconceptions.correction: There has to be an ordering quantity, and before protons were discovered atomic weight was the only one available. The groups emerged because similar properties recurred at regular intervals along that order.

misconceptions.question: Do isotopes give an element more than one atomic number?
misconceptions.correct: Isotopes of an element all have the same atomic number; they differ in the number of neutrons.
misconceptions.misconception: Because isotopes have different masses, the element has more than one atomic number, and that is what broke the early ordering.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know isotopes make mass ambiguous, and mass and atomic number sit side by side on the table, so the ambiguity gets attached to the wrong quantity.
misconceptions.correction: Atomic number is the proton count and is fixed for an element. It is the relative atomic mass that varies, because it is an average across the isotopes present - which is exactly why the order based on atomic weights was not always correct.

misconceptions.question: How do the boiling points of the noble gases change down Group 0?
misconceptions.correct: They increase with increasing relative atomic mass, going down the group.
misconceptions.misconception: Boiling point falls down the group, because the elements are gases and gases get harder to condense the further down you go.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate 'noble gas' with 'always a gas' and expect the gassiest behaviour lowest down. Some also carry the Group 7 reactivity trend across and assume every trend falls.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is explicit: boiling points increase with increasing relative atomic mass going down the group. Helium boils near −269 °C, argon near −186 °C, and the trend continues downwards.

misconceptions.question: If non-metals do not form positive ions, can they form ions at all?
misconceptions.correct: Non-metals do not form positive ions, but many form negative ions.
misconceptions.misconception: Non-metals are the elements that do not form ions, so a non-metal is always uncharged in a compound.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The definition is stated as a negative - 'do not form positive ions' - and the word 'positive' drops out when students summarise it.
misconceptions.correction: The word positive is load-bearing. Chlorine is a non-metal and forms chloride ions with a 1- charge in sodium chloride. What non-metals never do is form positive ions.

misconceptions.question: Do elements in the same group have the same number of electrons?
misconceptions.correct: They have the same number of outer electrons, not the same total.
misconceptions.misconception: Elements in a group behave alike because their atoms contain the same number of electrons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Same number of electrons' is the short version students carry away, and the word 'outer' is dropped as an unnecessary detail.
misconceptions.correction: A lithium atom has 3 electrons and a sodium atom has 11, yet both are in Group 1 - because both have one electron in the outer shell. It is the outer electrons that give similar chemical properties.

misconceptions.question: Are all the Group 7 elements gases at room temperature?
misconceptions.correct: Chlorine is a gas, bromine a liquid and iodine a solid at room temperature.
misconceptions.misconception: The halogens are all gases, because chlorine is a gas and they are all in the same group.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Chlorine is the halogen students meet first and it is a gas, so it becomes the template for the group. Similar properties are read as identical properties.
misconceptions.correction: Melting and boiling points rise down Group 7, so the state at room temperature changes as you go down: chlorine gas, bromine liquid, iodine solid. Astatine, lower still, would be predicted to be a solid.

misconceptions.question: Which ion does a metal atom form?
misconceptions.correct: A positive ion, formed by losing outer electrons.
misconceptions.misconception: Metal atoms gain electrons to fill their outer shell, like every other atom, so they end up negative.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule students internalise is 'atoms want a full outer shell', and gaining electrons is the only route they picture to filling one. Losing electrons to leave an empty shell behind feels like the wrong direction.
misconceptions.correction: A metal atom has few outer electrons, so losing them is far easier than gaining a full set. Losing electrons leaves more protons than electrons, hence a positive ion: magnesium loses two and forms a 2+ ion.

misconceptions.question: Were the problems with ordering by atomic weight caused by inaccurate measurements?
misconceptions.correct: Knowledge of isotopes explained the problem: relative atomic mass is an average and does not always rise with proton number.
misconceptions.misconception: The early chemists just weighed things badly, and better equipment sorted the table out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students assume any anomaly in old science is experimental error, and 'old apparatus was poor' is a familiar explanation that usually works.
misconceptions.correction: The weights were essentially right. Because an element's relative atomic mass is an average across its isotopes, a heavier element can have the lower proton number - which is precisely what knowledge of isotopes made it possible to explain.

misconceptions.question: Do all metals react with water the way sodium does?
misconceptions.correct: Only some metals react with water; Group 1 metals react vigorously because their single outer electron is lost easily.
misconceptions.misconception: Metals are reactive, so any metal dropped into water will fizz and react.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The sodium-in-water demonstration is memorable and is often the first metal reaction students see, so it becomes what metals do.
misconceptions.correction: Reactivity depends on how readily the atom loses outer electrons, which depends on position in the table. Group 1 metals, on the far left, react vigorously; copper, in the transition block, does not react with water.

misconceptions.question: Is the periodic table split roughly half metals and half non-metals?
misconceptions.correct: The majority of elements are metals; non-metals occupy only the top right.
misconceptions.misconception: There is a line down the middle of the table with metals on one side and non-metals on the other, in about equal numbers.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The stepped dividing line on many printed tables looks central, and 'metals and non-metals' as a pair of categories suggests a balanced split.
misconceptions.correction: The dividing line is far to the right and the whole transition block, plus the entire left-hand side and the bottom of the table, is metal. Metals are a clear majority.

misconceptions.question: Is the solution formed when an alkali metal reacts with water acidic?
misconceptions.correct: It is alkaline - a solution of the metal hydroxide.
misconceptions.misconception: The reaction is violent, so the solution left behind must be a strong acid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students link 'vigorous and dangerous' with 'acid', the substance they most associate with hazard, and lose track of the name alkali metal.
misconceptions.correction: They are called the alkali metals for this reason: sodium and water give sodium hydroxide solution, which is alkaline and turns universal indicator purple.

misconceptions.question: Is hydrogen given off whenever an alkali metal reacts?
misconceptions.correct: Hydrogen is released in the reaction with water only; with oxygen an oxide forms, and with chlorine a chloride.
misconceptions.misconception: Alkali metals always give off hydrogen gas, whatever they are reacting with.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The reaction with water is the one demonstrated, and its fizzing is the strongest memory of Group 1, so hydrogen becomes attached to the metal rather than to the water.
misconceptions.correction: Track the atoms available. Lithium heated in oxygen gives lithium oxide only (4Li + O2 -> 2Li2O) - there is no hydrogen in the reaction to be released.

misconceptions.question: If there are more protons further down a group, does the pull on the outer electrons get stronger?
misconceptions.correct: The extra inner shells increase the distance and the shielding, so the overall attraction on the outer electrons is weaker.
misconceptions.misconception: More protons means a bigger nuclear charge, so lower elements hold their outer electrons more tightly.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The statement about nuclear charge is true on its own, and students apply it without weighing the two effects that work against it - greater distance and more shielding by inner shells.
misconceptions.correction: Down a group, the outer shell is further from the nucleus and shielded by more inner shells, and these outweigh the rise in nuclear charge. That is why Group 1 loses its outer electron more easily further down and Group 7 gains one less easily.

misconceptions.question: Do displacement reactions only happen with metals?
misconceptions.correct: Halogens displace one another too: a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from an aqueous solution of its salt.
misconceptions.misconception: Displacement is about a reactive metal pushing out a less reactive metal, so two non-metal solutions will not react at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Displacement is usually taught first with the metal reactivity series, so the idea gets tied to metals rather than to the general principle of a more reactive element taking the place of a less reactive one.
misconceptions.correction: The same competition applies within Group 7. Chlorine added to potassium bromide solution displaces bromine: Cl2 + 2KBr -> 2KCl + Br2, and the solution turns orange as bromine forms.

mcqs.stem: In the modern periodic table, the elements are placed in order of which quantity?

options.text: Atomic (proton) number, increasing across each period
options.rationale: The specification states that elements are arranged in order of atomic (proton) number, which rises by one from each element to the next.

options.text: Relative atomic mass, rising steadily across each period
options.rationale: Relative atomic mass is printed on the table and usually does rise left to right, and it is the quantity the earliest tables really used, so it looks like the ordering rule.

options.text: The number of electrons in the outer shell of every atom
options.rationale: Students who know that outer electrons decide the groups assume they must also decide the overall order, but outer electrons repeat 1 to 8 rather than increasing.

options.text: The number of neutrons in the nucleus of a single atom
options.rationale: Neutron number is confused with proton number because both are nuclear particles, but neutron number varies between isotopes of the same element.

mcqs.stem: Why is the table of the elements described as a periodic table?

options.text: Every period contains exactly the same number of elements
options.rationale: Students read 'periodic' as being about the periods themselves, and equal-length rows sounds like the tidiest version of that; in fact periods differ in length.

options.text: Elements with similar properties recur at regular intervals
options.rationale: This is the specification's own reason: similar properties occur at regular intervals as atomic number increases, which is what periodic means.

options.text: Each period holds elements with identical outer electrons
options.rationale: This is the group and period swap: it correctly describes the columns, but attaches the property to the rows.

options.text: The properties of every element repeat exactly one row later
options.rationale: An over-literal reading of 'regular intervals' as 'every single row', which ignores that the intervals lengthen further down the table.

mcqs.stem: Fluorine and chlorine are both in Group 7. Why do they have similar chemical properties?

options.text: Their atoms contain the same total number of electrons
options.rationale: The word 'outer' is dropped from the rule; fluorine atoms have 9 electrons and chlorine atoms 17, so the totals differ.

options.text: Their atoms have the same number of occupied shells
options.rationale: Group and period are swapped. Fluorine is in Period 2 and chlorine in Period 3, so the shell counts are not the same.

options.text: Their atoms both have seven electrons in the outer shell
options.rationale: Elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons, and it is the outer electrons that determine chemical behaviour.

options.text: Their atoms have equal numbers of neutrons and protons
options.rationale: A half-remembered fact about light nuclei is offered as the reason; nuclear composition does not control chemical properties.

mcqs.stem: An atom of an element has the electronic structure 2,8,7. Where is this element found in the periodic table?

options.text: Group 3, Period 7
options.rationale: The two numbers are read the wrong way round, the classic group and period swap.

options.text: Group 7, Period 2
options.rationale: The outer electrons are counted correctly but the shells are miscounted, often by treating 2,8 as a single inner shell.

options.text: Group 8, Period 3
options.rationale: The student takes the full shell of 8 as the outer shell and reads off the wrong figure; the outer shell is the last one listed, holding 7.

options.text: Group 7, Period 3
options.rationale: Seven outer electrons place it in Group 7; three occupied shells place it in Period 3. The element is chlorine.

mcqs.stem: An element is in Group 2 and Period 3. What is the electronic structure of an atom of this element?

options.rationale: Three occupied shells for Period 3 and two outer electrons for Group 2, giving magnesium, atomic number 12.
Group and period are swapped, producing an atom of Group 3, Period 2 instead.
One shell too many: the student fills up to the fourth shell, which would be Period 4 (calcium), not Period 3.
The period number is used as the outer electron count, so the group is misread as 3.

mcqs.stem: Sodium reacts vigorously with water. Which element would be expected to react with water in a similar way?

options.text: Magnesium, because it sits next to sodium
options.rationale: Neighbours along a period are treated as the family. Magnesium has two outer electrons and reacts far more slowly with water.

options.text: Potassium, because it is also in Group 1
options.rationale: Elements in the same group react in the same sort of way; potassium has one outer electron like sodium, so it too reacts vigorously with water.

options.text: Copper, because copper is a metal as well
options.rationale: All metals are assumed to behave like the memorable sodium demonstration; copper does not react with water at all.

options.text: Neon, because it lies in sodium's period
options.rationale: Position in the same region of the table is mistaken for similar chemistry; neon is a noble gas and is unreactive.

mcqs.stem: Before protons, neutrons and electrons had been discovered, how did scientists attempt to classify the elements?

options.text: By arranging them in order of atomic number
options.rationale: Atomic number is such a basic idea now that students assume it was always available; it could not be used before protons were found.

options.text: By arranging them in order of melting point
options.rationale: Melting point was measurable at the time, so this sounds plausible, but it produces no repeating pattern of properties.

options.text: By arranging them in order of atomic weight
options.rationale: Atomic weight was the only measurable quantity that ordered the elements before subatomic particles were known.

options.text: By arranging them in order of how reactive
options.rationale: Grouping by observed behaviour feels like the obvious first step, but reactivity is a comparison, not a quantity that can order every element.

mcqs.stem: Why did following the strict order of atomic weights cause problems in the early periodic tables?

options.text: It gave several elements the wrong atomic number
options.rationale: Atomic numbers are assumed to have existed at the time; they were unknown, so they could not be got wrong.

options.text: It made all of the groups contain unequal numbers
options.rationale: Unequal group sizes look untidy, but the real problem was elements sitting with elements they did not resemble.

options.text: It left no room for new elements to be added
options.rationale: This confuses the problem with the solution: it was Mendeleev's gaps that made room, and the tables were incomplete rather than closed.

options.text: It placed some elements in groups they did not fit
options.rationale: The specification states that some elements were placed in inappropriate groups if the strict order of atomic weights was followed.

mcqs.stem: Why did Mendeleev leave gaps in his periodic table?

options.text: He thought elements filling them had not been found yet
options.rationale: The gaps were predictions. Elements with the properties Mendeleev predicted were later discovered and filled them.

options.text: He could not decide where some known elements belonged
options.rationale: The gaps are read as indecision rather than prediction; the elements Mendeleev could not place by weight he reordered, not omitted.

options.text: He wanted each of his groups to contain equal numbers
options.rationale: The finished table looks neat, so tidiness is offered as the motive rather than a scientific prediction.

options.text: He was waiting for the atomic numbers to be measured
options.rationale: Atomic number is assumed to have been just around the corner; protons had not been discovered when he built the table.

mcqs.stem: How did knowledge of isotopes explain why the order based on atomic weights was not always correct?

options.text: Isotopes give an element two different atomic numbers
options.rationale: The ambiguity isotopes create is attached to atomic number instead of to mass; isotopes of an element share one atomic number.

options.text: An element's mass is an average across its isotopes
options.rationale: Because relative atomic mass averages isotopes according to their abundance, an element can have a greater mass but a smaller proton number, breaking the weight order.

options.text: Isotopes were weighed inaccurately by early chemists
options.rationale: Any anomaly in old science is assumed to be measurement error, but the atomic weights were essentially correct.

options.text: Isotopes exist only in the elements Mendeleev swapped
options.rationale: Isotopes are treated as a rare special case created to excuse the anomalies, rather than as something most elements have.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about Mendeleev's periodic table is correct?

options.text: He arranged the elements by their atomic numbers
options.rationale: His table resembles the modern one, so students assume the modern ordering rule; he used atomic weights.

options.text: He left gaps to make the table look symmetrical
options.rationale: The neat appearance of the table is taken as the purpose of the gaps rather than as a by-product of the prediction.

options.text: He changed the order of some pairs of elements
options.rationale: Where atomic weight order clashed with properties, Mendeleev changed the order so that elements sat with those they resembled.

options.text: He included all of the noble gases in his table
options.rationale: Group 0 is so familiar from modern tables that it is assumed to have always been there; the noble gases had not yet been discovered.

mcqs.stem: Which statement gives the chemical definition of a metal used in the periodic table?

options.text: An element that conducts electricity and heat
options.rationale: The easiest physical test is mistaken for the definition. Graphite, a form of carbon, conducts electricity but carbon is a non-metal.

options.text: An element that reacts to produce negative ions
options.rationale: The charge is reversed by students who think every atom fills its outer shell by gaining electrons.

options.text: An element that is shiny and can be beaten flat
options.rationale: Appearance and malleability are typical of metals, so they get promoted from evidence to definition.

options.text: An element that reacts to form positive ions
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition; elements that do not form positive ions are non-metals.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the positions of metals and non-metals in the periodic table is correct?

options.text: Most elements are metals, found left and towards the bottom
options.rationale: The majority of elements are metals, and they lie to the left and towards the bottom of the table.

options.text: Most elements are non-metals, found right and towards the top
options.rationale: The non-metals dominate early chemistry lessons, so students overestimate how many there are; the positions given are right but the majority is wrong.

options.text: Metals and non-metals are split evenly down the middle
options.rationale: The stepped dividing line looks central on a printed table, suggesting an equal share on each side.

options.text: Non-metals are found only in the bottom right of the table
options.rationale: The correct corner is remembered but the wrong vertical direction; non-metals sit towards the top right, and metals towards the bottom.

mcqs.stem: Which property is characteristic of non-metals rather than metals?

options.text: Good conduction of an electric current
options.rationale: Conductivity is a metallic property, but students who define metals by conductivity can lose track of which side it belongs to.

options.text: Generally low melting and boiling points
options.rationale: Non-metals generally melt and boil at lower temperatures than metals, one of their characteristic physical properties.

options.text: Forming positive ions during a reaction
options.rationale: The ion charges are reversed; forming positive ions is precisely what makes an element a metal.

options.text: Malleable when hammered into shape
options.rationale: Malleability is metallic; non-metal solids are typically brittle and shatter when hammered.

mcqs.stem: Why are the elements on the far left of the periodic table metals?

options.text: Their atoms have the fewest occupied electron shells
options.rationale: Position from left to right is explained using shells, which actually set the period; Group 1 runs from Period 2 right down the table.

options.text: Their atoms gain electrons to fill their outer shell
options.rationale: The 'atoms want a full shell' rule is applied without noticing that losing one or two electrons is the easier route here.

options.text: Their atoms have few outer electrons and lose them
options.rationale: Few outer electrons are lost far more easily than a full set is gained, so these atoms form positive ions - the definition of a metal.

options.text: Their atoms carry no charge and cannot form any ions
options.rationale: Neutral atoms are confused with an inability to form ions; metal atoms are neutral until they lose electrons.

mcqs.stem: Magnesium is in Group 2 of the periodic table. Which ion does a magnesium atom form, and why?

options.text: A 2- ion, because its atom gains two outer electrons
options.rationale: The 'fill the outer shell by gaining' rule is applied to a metal, reversing the charge.

options.text: A 3+ ion, because it lies in the third period
options.rationale: The period number is used in place of the group number to fix the charge.

options.text: A 1+ ion, because atoms lose just one electron
options.rationale: The Group 1 case is generalised into a rule that atoms only ever transfer a single electron.

options.text: A 2+ ion, because its atom loses two outer electrons
options.rationale: Group 2 means two outer electrons; losing both leaves two more protons than electrons, giving a 2+ ion.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the outer shell of the noble gas atoms is correct?

options.text: All have eight outer electrons except helium, which has two
options.rationale: This is exactly what the specification states, including the helium exception.

options.text: All of them have eight electrons in their outer shell
options.rationale: The 'stable octet' is treated as a rule without exceptions, and helium is quietly included.

options.text: All of them have an empty outer shell of electrons
options.rationale: Unreactive is read as 'nothing there to react', so the full shell becomes an empty one.

options.text: All have two outer electrons except helium, which has eight
options.rationale: The exception is remembered but applied the wrong way round, to the whole group instead of to helium.

mcqs.stem: Why are the elements in Group 0 unreactive?

options.text: Their atoms have no electrons in the outer shell to give away
options.rationale: 'Does not give electrons away' is turned into 'has none to give', replacing a full shell with an empty one.

options.text: Their atoms already have a stable arrangement of electrons
options.rationale: A full outer shell is stable, so there is nothing to be gained by losing, gaining or sharing electrons.

options.text: Their atoms are held together as extremely stable molecules
options.rationale: Stability is attributed to bonding between atoms; in fact the noble gases do not easily form molecules at all.

options.text: Their atoms all contain exactly the same number of electrons
options.rationale: 'Same number of electrons' is carried over from the rule about groups, dropping the word outer, and helium and argon plainly differ.

mcqs.stem: How do the boiling points of the noble gases change going down Group 0?

options.text: They decrease as the relative atomic mass gets larger
options.rationale: 'Noble gas' is read as 'always more gas-like lower down', so the trend is reversed.

options.text: They are identical because all these atoms are stable
options.rationale: Chemical stability is assumed to make the elements physically alike, so no trend is expected.

options.text: They increase as the relative atomic mass increases
options.rationale: The specification states that boiling points increase with increasing relative atomic mass, going down the group.

options.text: They rise as far as argon and then fall away below it
options.rationale: The three familiar values are recalled and a peak is invented beyond them; the trend continues to rise.

mcqs.stem: The boiling points of three noble gases are helium −269 °C, neon −246 °C and argon −186 °C. Krypton is the next element down the group. Which value is the best prediction for the boiling point of krypton?

options.rationale: The trend is read as falling, so a value below helium's is chosen.
The direction of the trend is ignored and a value is interpolated between neon and argon rather than extended beyond argon.
The noble gases are assumed to behave identically, so krypton is given the same value as argon.
The trend rises down the group, so krypton must boil above argon's −186 °C; only this value does.

mcqs.stem: Why do the elements in Group 1 have similar chemical properties?

options.text: Each atom has a single electron in its outer shell
options.rationale: The characteristic properties of the alkali metals come from that one outer electron, which is lost in reactions.

options.text: Each atom contains the same number of electrons
options.rationale: The word outer is dropped; lithium atoms have 3 electrons and sodium atoms 11.

options.text: Each atom has the same number of occupied shells
options.rationale: The property that defines a period is used to explain a group.

options.text: Each atom loses all of its electrons in a reaction
options.rationale: 'Loses electrons' is over-extended to all of them; only the single outer electron is lost.

mcqs.stem: Potassium is added to water. What are the products of the reaction?

options.text: Potassium hydroxide solution and oxygen gas
options.rationale: The gas is assumed to be oxygen released from the water; the oxygen in fact stays in the hydroxide.

options.text: Potassium hydroxide solution and hydrogen gas
options.rationale: Alkali metals react with water to give the metal hydroxide in solution and hydrogen: 2K + 2H2O -> 2KOH + H2.

options.text: Potassium oxide and hydrogen gas are produced
options.rationale: The reaction with oxygen is confused with the reaction with water; potassium oxide would not be the product in water.

options.text: Potassium hydride and an acidic solution are made
options.rationale: A violent reaction is assumed to leave an acid; the alkali metals are so named because the solution is alkaline.

mcqs.stem: Which equation correctly represents the reaction of sodium with chlorine?

options.text: Na + Cl -> NaCl
options.rationale: Chlorine gas is written as single atoms, copying the symbol on the periodic table rather than the diatomic molecule.

options.text: Na + Cl2 -> NaCl2
options.rationale: The molecule is kept intact and the formula adjusted around it, which requires sodium to form a 2+ ion; a Group 1 atom loses only one electron.

options.text: 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl
options.rationale: Chlorine is diatomic and sodium chloride is NaCl, so two sodium atoms are needed to balance the two chlorine atoms.

options.text: 2Na + Cl2 -> Na2Cl
options.rationale: The 2 in front of Na is carried into the formula of the product, giving a compound with the wrong ratio of ions.

mcqs.stem: A small piece of lithium is heated strongly in oxygen. What is formed?

options.text: Lithium oxide, LiO2, a white powder
options.rationale: The name is right but the formula requires a 2+ lithium ion; a Group 1 atom loses one electron, so two are needed per oxide ion.

options.text: Lithium oxide, Li2O, plus hydrogen gas
options.rationale: Hydrogen is attached to alkali metals generally, from the memorable reaction with water; there is no hydrogen in this reaction.

options.text: Lithium hydroxide, LiOH, plus water
options.rationale: The products of the reaction with water are recalled instead of those of burning in oxygen.

options.text: Lithium oxide, Li2O, a white solid
options.rationale: Alkali metals burn in oxygen to form the metal oxide: 4Li + O2 -> 2Li2O, a white solid.

mcqs.stem: Why does the reactivity of the Group 1 elements increase going down the group?

options.text: The outer electron is further away and so is lost more easily
options.rationale: Greater distance from the nucleus and shielding by more inner shells weaken the attraction on the single outer electron, so it is lost more readily.

options.text: Each atom lower down the group has more electrons it can lose
options.rationale: Larger atoms are assumed to donate more electrons; every Group 1 atom loses exactly one.

options.text: The nucleus contains more protons and pulls the electron in
options.rationale: A true fact about nuclear charge is applied without weighing distance and shielding, which outweigh it - and it predicts the opposite trend.

options.text: The atoms lower down have more electrons in the outer shell
options.rationale: The rising total electron count is misread as a rising outer shell count, which would change the group.

mcqs.stem: Rubidium lies below potassium in Group 1. Predict how rubidium reacts with water.

options.text: Less vigorously than potassium, giving off hydrogen
options.rationale: The rise in nuclear charge is assumed to hold the outer electron more tightly, reversing the trend.

options.text: More vigorously than potassium, giving off hydrogen
options.rationale: Reactivity increases down Group 1, so rubidium reacts more vigorously; the products are still the hydroxide and hydrogen.

options.text: More vigorously than potassium, giving off oxygen
options.rationale: The trend is applied correctly but the gas is misidentified as oxygen from the water.

options.text: About the same as potassium, giving off no gas at all
options.rationale: Similar properties within a group are read as identical, and the fizzing is overlooked.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the elements in Group 7 is correct?

options.text: They are non-metals that exist as separate single atoms
options.rationale: The single symbol printed on the periodic table is taken as the formula of the free element.

options.text: They are non-metals with one electron in the outer shell
options.rationale: The Group 1 arrangement is applied to Group 7; halogen atoms have seven outer electrons.

options.text: They are non-metals whose molecules contain two atoms
options.rationale: The halogens are non-metals and consist of molecules made of pairs of atoms, such as Cl2, Br2 and I2.

options.text: They are metals that form molecules containing two atoms
options.rationale: Forming salts with metals leads students to classify the halogens as metallic themselves.

mcqs.stem: Chlorine reacts with sodium and it also reacts with hydrogen. What types of compound are formed?

options.text: Covalent with sodium and ionic with hydrogen gas
options.rationale: The two partners are swapped by a student who has not linked bonding type to whether the partner is a metal.

options.text: Covalent with sodium and covalent with hydrogen
options.rationale: Chlorine is a non-metal, so it is assumed never to form ions at all; chloride ions form readily with metals.

options.text: Ionic with sodium and also ionic with hydrogen
options.rationale: The ionic case is generalised to every partner, ignoring that two non-metals share electrons instead.

options.text: Ionic with sodium and covalent with hydrogen
options.rationale: A halogen forms ionic compounds with metals and covalent, molecular compounds with non-metals; sodium is a metal and hydrogen a non-metal.

mcqs.stem: Astatine lies below iodine in Group 7. Iodine is a solid at room temperature. What can be predicted about astatine at room temperature?

options.text: A solid, because melting point rises down the group
options.rationale: Melting and boiling points increase down Group 7, so an element below iodine must also be a solid at room temperature.

options.text: A gas, because all of the Group 7 elements are gases
options.rationale: Chlorine is the halogen met first and it is a gas, so the whole group is assumed to be gaseous.

options.text: A gas, because it is the most reactive of the halogens
options.rationale: The reactivity trend is reversed and then, wrongly, used to predict a physical state.

options.text: A liquid, because it comes just after iodine in the group
options.rationale: The states are assumed to cycle gas, liquid, solid and then begin again, rather than following a one-way trend.

mcqs.stem: Why does the reactivity of the Group 7 elements decrease going down the group?

options.text: Heavier atoms simply move around more slowly and so react less
options.rationale: Mass is used as the explanation because it is the most obvious difference down the group, but it is not the cause.

options.text: Gaining an electron is harder as the outer shell is further out
options.rationale: The outer shell is further from the nucleus and shielded by more inner shells, so an electron is attracted into it less strongly.

options.text: More protons in the nucleus hold the outer shell more tightly
options.rationale: Nuclear charge is considered alone; it does rise, but distance and shielding outweigh it, and this reasoning would make gaining an electron easier.

options.text: Atoms further down the group lose their outer electrons easily
options.rationale: The Group 1 explanation is transferred wholesale; halogens gain an electron rather than losing one.

mcqs.stem: Chlorine solution is added to potassium bromide solution. What happens?

options.text: The bromine displaces chlorine from the solution
options.rationale: Bromine is taken to be the more reactive because its atoms are larger and heavier.

options.text: The halogens swap over to form bromine chloride
options.rationale: Displacement is pictured as the two halogens combining rather than one taking the other's place in the salt.

options.text: The chlorine displaces bromine from the solution
options.rationale: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so it displaces it from a solution of its salt: Cl2 + 2KBr -> 2KCl + Br2.

options.text: No reaction occurs between these two solutions
options.rationale: Displacement is thought to belong to metals only, so no reaction is expected between non-metals.

mcqs.stem: Bromine water is added to potassium chloride solution in one tube and to potassium iodide solution in another. What is observed?

options.text: It reacts with both, releasing chlorine and iodine
options.rationale: Displacement is treated as an automatic swap whenever a halogen meets a halide, with no check on reactivity.

options.text: It reacts with the chloride only, releasing chlorine
options.rationale: The reactivity order is reversed, so bromine is thought to beat chlorine but not iodine.

options.text: It reacts with neither of the two halide solutions
options.rationale: Displacement is assumed to require a metal, so no reaction is expected in either tube.

options.text: It reacts with the iodide only, releasing iodine
options.rationale: Bromine is more reactive than iodine but less reactive than chlorine, so it displaces iodide but not chloride: Br2 + 2KI -> 2KBr + I2.
